name: kelmar
author: weather-and-seasons designer
description:
kelmar v3 (direction: weather and seasons) -- RAIN OVER A GARDEN: THE PLANTS THAT LEAN OUT FOR A
DRINK. PRIVATE; never shown to players. Previous versions: challenges/lab/kelmar.v1.json (0 % for
four Opus players; clue was a string plus a legend) and challenges/lab/kelmar.v2.json (mean 5 %
over eight Opus players; 9 % with a demo, 0 % without).

WHY v3. In v2 the clue was an EMPTY sky over a garden and the answer was the rain the player had to
invent. Every player report says the same thing: nobody ever saw rain. "dot rows replaced by blocks
of | (identical on every row), ground line kept, number line dropped; the block geometry is still
unexplained" (dornic1b, two demos spent). "vertical stripes of ' (grass) and . repeated on every
blank row: 3 on / 3 off" (tovel3b, 20 % from a stripe template). "N evenly spaced 3-wide bands,
glyph |, 5/18 on num=2 clues" (dornic1a). "solid | blocks in the sky ... the geometry is not yet
cracked" (tovel3a). Two players spent a demo and still described the picture as blocks; the players
who spent none tried ~18 edits for 0/825. The clause nobody ever conceived was the whole rule --
that the number counts PLANTS, in a relation to the rain. The rain was the answer, so it read as an
arbitrary pattern to be reverse-engineered, and the plants (in the clue, unchanged by the answer)
looked like decoration.

v3 turns the picture round, fennick-style: THE RAIN IS IN THE CLUE AND THE ANSWER EDITS THE PLANTS.
  * the clue is a finished weather picture: a cloud row, K rows of falling drops, the garden row,
    and a caption "<n> lean" that names the verb (fennick's "n fall");
  * the answer is that same picture with exactly the right plants drawn leaning ("/" or "\");
  * the caption is a free checksum: a team can test a candidate rule against ~80 harvested clues in
    round 1 without answering anything, which is how fennick's two crackers cracked fennick.

CLUE and ANSWER, seed 44 (a typical demo):

    ..(~~)....(~~~).....(~)....(~)...(~~)....      ..(~~)....(~~~).....(~)....(~)...(~~)....
    ..''''....'''''.....'''....'''...''''....      ..''''....'''''.....'''....'''...''''....
    ..''''....'''''.....'''....'''...''''....  ->  ..''''....'''''.....'''....'''...''''....
    ..''''....'''''..................''''....      ..''''....'''''..................''''....
    __*_*_Y_Y___*_Y____*____Y_Y_*___*___*_Y__      __*_*_\_Y___*_Y____*____Y_Y_*___/___*_Y__
    2 lean                                         2 lean

Three showers reach the ground (columns 2-5, 10-14, 33-36) and two stop in the air (20-22, 27-29).
The tree at column 6 and the flower at column 32 are the two plants standing dry right beside rain
that lands, so they lean towards it. Everything else stays upright, and the picture says why: two
flowers stand IN the rain, one flower stands right beside the hanging shower at 20-22, one stands
directly UNDER the hanging shower at 27-29, one tree is two columns clear, and several are nowhere
near any rain.

W = 32-42 columns. A cloud "(~~~)" sits over each shower; under it fall K rows of drops ("'"),
K = 3 or 4. A shower either REACHES THE GROUND (drops in all K rows, i.e. in the row immediately
above the garden) or STOPS IN THE AIR (drops in only 1..K-1 rows). Every clue has 2-3 showers that
land and at least 2 that hang. The garden row is bare earth "_" carrying 9-15 plants -- flowers "*"
and small trees "Y", at least 2 of each, at least 2 columns apart, never in the outer column.
Showers are 3-5 wide with at least 3 dry columns between them, so no plant is ever beside two
showers at once.

THE RULE, the sentence a kid says while pointing: A PLANT LEANS OVER FOR A DRINK IF THE RAIN RIGHT
NEXT TO IT COMES ALL THE WAY DOWN TO THE GROUND. Formally: exactly those plants whose own column is
dry in the bottom row of drops and whose left or right neighbouring column is wet in that row.
A plant standing IN the rain does not lean (it does not need to); a plant standing under -- or
beside -- rain that stops in mid air does not lean (that rain never gets to it); a plant two or more
columns clear does not lean. Flowers and trees are not told apart: the two glyphs are a decoy
dimension that the caption's checksum kills in one round. The leaning plant is drawn "/" if the rain
is on its right and "\" if the rain is on its left -- the picture points at its own law -- but the
scorer accepts either glyph, so a team that has the right plants and the wrong tilt still scores.

ANSWER = the clue's picture with exactly those plants replaced by a lean glyph. The cloud row and
the drop rows must be copied unchanged, the garden row must be copied except at the leaning plants,
and the "<n> lean" line may be kept or dropped (house rule). Blank lines around the picture and
trailing spaces are ignored. The answer is UNIQUE up to the two lean glyphs, so the class cannot be
shotgunned: a "several candidate garden rows in one answer" attack scores 0.0 %.

THE FOOTHOLD (lever 7). 12.3 % of clues say "0 lean" -- no shower that lands has a plant beside it,
and the correct answer IS the clue's picture returned unchanged. A demo-less team that echoes the
picture scores 12 %, exactly fennick's floor, and learns from the caption that the class is
picture-graded rather than exact-match.

WHAT EVERY DEMO SHOWS (measured over 4000 clues). A plant standing in landing rain, upright: 100 %.
A plant standing directly under rain that stops in the air, upright: 100 %. A plant standing beside
rain that stops in the air, upright: 96.4 % (two or more of them: 88.7 %). A plant far from all rain,
upright: 100 %. At least one leaning plant: 87.7 %; a leaner and an upright plant-beside-hanging-rain
within 8 columns of each other: 63.3 %; a leaner and a wet plant within 8 columns: 96.9 %. So a
single demo shows the positive case and all three near misses side by side, and the one dimension
that matters -- how far down the drops come -- varies inside every picture.

WITNESS TABLE (2000 fresh clues; every attacker except the echoes knows the drawing convention,
i.e. it models a player who has seen a demo and holds the wrong rule):
  the TRUE rule (solve)                                       100.0 %
  the n plants nearest rain that lands (= the rule restated)  100.0 %
  only the TREES beside landing rain                           43.4 %
  only the FLOWERS beside landing rain                         40.8 %
  the n plants nearest ANY rain, leftmost ties                 39.9 %
  the n plants nearest ANY rain, random ties                   32.6 %
  within 2 columns of landing rain                             20.6 %
  n random plants / the n leftmost plants                      16.4 / 16.2 %
  the clue echoed unchanged (the foothold)                     12.2 %
  the clue's picture with the caption dropped                  12.2 %
  beside ANY rain, the hanging showers counted too              4.0 %
  beside hanging rain only                                      0.2 %
  within 2 of any rain / under hanging rain / in the rain       0.0 %
  every dry plant / every plant                                 0.0 %
  shotgun (22 candidate garden rows in one answer)              0.0 %
  the edited garden row alone / rain redrawn as "|"             0.0 %
  demo replay / one constant answer / empty / 4000 chars junk   0.0 %
Nothing insight-free beats 17 %, and those entries are the 12 % echo plus luck. The 33-43 % band
is the intended partial tier: a player who reads the picture as rain and uses the caption's count,
but has not noticed that some showers never reach the ground, marks the n plants nearest any rain
and lands there. A player who has the landing insight but restricts it to one kind of plant sits at
~41 % and is told so by the checksum on half the clues.

FAIRNESS FLOOR. Of 20 hand-built "the caption counts THIS relation" laws, on shipped demos: 3.8
survive one demo, 2.0 survive two, 1.4 survive three, and in 267/400 trials exactly one law survives
three demos and it is the true rule. The caption makes this far cheaper than it looks: the count can
be checked against every harvested clue for free, so a team that enumerates plant/rain relations at
all kills the field in round 1 without spending an answer. The whole difficulty is looking at how far
down the drops come.

VALIDATION. quickcheck --seeds 200: OK, no warnings. 4000 fresh seeds: generate deterministic,
4000/4000 distinct, mean 0.13 ms, no fallback; solve() scores 1 on 4000/4000, mean 0.006 ms; score
mean 0.009 ms, worst 0.043 ms on junk. Scorer vs an independent re-implementation (column walk, no
regex) on 49500 (clue, answer) pairs -- shipped demos plus 33 structural mutations each: 0
disagreements. Junk (17 strings x 500 clues plus clue fragments): 0 raises, 0 non-binary returns,
0 false positives. Sizes: score 415/512, solve 348, generate 2792; clue 171-264 chars, solution
171-264. Lenient, all 100 %: caption kept or dropped, leading/trailing blank lines, rows
right-padded, CRLF, either lean glyph, both glyphs swapped. Strict, all 0 %: dry sky redrawn with
spaces, rain redrawn as "|", cloud row dropped, an extra sky row, the garden row alone, a leaning
plant straightened, one extra plant leaned, leans drawn as "v", a text label added, rows reversed,
the picture shifted one column.

PREDICTED CLASSIFICATION: testing, mean final 40-65 %; the risk is now too_easy, not too_hard.
Levers if it comes back over 0.8: (1) make the reach depend on the plant -- a tree leans from two
columns away, a flower only from one (measured on a variant: the "n nearest" template drops to
~60 %, and the species split costs a round); (2) draw some showers slanting, so the drink is only
available downwind; (3) drop the caption's count to a "<n> lean" that counts showers instead of
plants. Levers if it comes back under 0.15: make every shower land except one (the virga clause
becomes a single visible exception), or put one leaning plant into the clue as a worked instance.

Design notes, the brainstorm and the full iteration record: challenges/lab/NOTES_weather.md.
